name: Pygmalion effect
statement: Tell a teacher that certain pupils are about to bloom and those pupils are said to improve, because the expectation changes how they are taught.
meaning: The claim is causal and it runs from the adult's belief to the child's measured ability. What makes it striking rather than obvious is the choice of measure: not grades, which a teacher marks, but IQ, which is supposed to be a property of the child. If a false belief planted in a teacher can move a pupil's IQ score, then intelligence is partly a social product, and the mechanism has to be something in the hundreds of small interactions a term is made of.

origin.where: the book Pygmalion in the Classroom
origin.note: In May 1964 the pupils of Oak School, an elementary school in South San Francisco where Jacobson was principal, sat the Tests of General Ability. Their own teachers administered it, and were told it was a Harvard test that predicted which children were about to spurt. That autumn each of the 18 teachers was handed a list of the children said to have scored in the top 20 percent, picked from a table of random numbers. Spitz and Rosenthal both record that the pretest was given a school year before the grade labels used in the results, so the children reported as first-graders sat it in kindergarten. The reasoning came from Rosenthal's earlier work on experimenter expectancy, where an experimenter's belief about a hypothesis shifts the results they obtain.

evidence: Teachers were given the names, the school year ran, and everyone was tested again. Both groups gained, the bloomers about 12 IQ points and the controls about 8. Jussim and Harber put numbers on the gap between them. It corresponded to an effect size of 0.30, a correlation of r = .15, and a mean difference in IQ gain of about four points. The effect was concentrated: significant in two of six grades in the first year and one of five in the second, which is to say absent in eight of the eleven grades examined. Thorndike's 1968 review reprints Rosenthal and Jacobson's own first-year table, and it shows where the concentration sits. Grade 1 gained 27.4 points for 7 bloomers against 12.0 for 48 controls, grade 2 gained 16.5 for 12 against 7.0 for 47, and the differences in grades 3 to 6 were 0.0, 3.4, minus 0.1 and minus 0.7. The first-year result therefore rests on 19 children. It also rests on a shrunken school. Elashoff and Snow counted 478 children given the pretest and 382, or 80 percent, present for at least one posttest and so counted as being in the experiment.

replication.headline: Eighteen experiments pooled to almost nothing, and the effect survives only where teachers had not yet met the children.
replication.detail: Raudenbush's meta-analysis of 18 experiments on induced teacher expectations and IQ found a mean of d = 0.11, small enough that whether it reached significance depended on which test he used. His abstract at the journal states the point of the exercise: the better teachers already knew their pupils when the false information arrived, the smaller the effect should be, and the data strongly support that. Spitz sets out the gradient. Four studies with no prior contact averaged d = 0.32, r = .16, three with one week 0.26, three with two weeks 0.08, and eight with more than two weeks minus 0.04. Eight of the 19 effect sizes were negative. Raudenbush also reported that effects exceeded zero only for low-contact studies in grades 1 and 2 and in grade 7. Re-analysing the same 18 studies with random-effects models in 1994, he reported d = 0.43 for the four experiments where teachers had no prior contact, a correlation of about r = .2, and no overall effect across the remaining fourteen. Jussim and Harber's review of 35 years of this literature concludes that classroom self-fulfilling prophecies do occur, that they are typically small, that they do not accumulate much across perceivers or over time, and that teacher expectations may predict pupil outcomes more because they are accurate than because they are self-fulfilling. Their summary is that the effect on IQ runs from nonexistent to small, and that the hypothesis of large and dramatic effects on IQ has been disconfirmed. Work since has left the false-information design behind in two directions. De Boer, Timmermans and van der Werf reviewed 19 interventions that tried to raise teacher expectations openly. Five carried enough data to pool for expectations, at Hedges' g = 0.38, SE 0.17, p = 0.023, 95 percent confidence interval 0.05 to 0.70, and seven for achievement, at g = 0.30, SE 0.11, p = 0.005, 95 percent confidence interval 0.09 to 0.51. Both pools were too small for moderator analysis, with I-squared of 58.8 and 80.3. The largest of them, Rubie-Davies and colleagues' year-long randomised workshop programme for primary teachers, raised the experimental pupils' maths gains and not their reading gains, which de Boer attributes to teachers using it more in maths lessons. The second direction is expectations that arose on their own. Gentrup and colleagues followed 1,026 first-graders in 64 German classrooms, from 1,065 in 67 recruited, and found that the part of a teacher's expectation not explained by a pupil's achievement, cognitive ability and motivation still predicted end-of-year attainment. In reading the standardised coefficients were 0.25 for inaccurately high expectations, p = .002, and minus 0.42 for inaccurately low ones, p < .001. In mathematics inaccurately high expectations gave 0.14, p = .014, and inaccurately low ones did not depress attainment at all. Rated teacher feedback, in a subsample of 19 classrooms and 354 pupils, varied with the inaccuracy and did not carry the effect.

study.cite: Raudenbush, S. W. (1984). Magnitude of teacher expectancy effects on pupil IQ as a function of the credibility of expectancy induction: A synthesis of findings from 18 experiments. Journal of Educational Psychology, 76(1), 85-97.

limits: The instrument is the oldest objection and it runs on the original authors' own numbers. Elashoff and Snow report Total IQ scores ranging from 39 to 202, Reasoning IQ from 0 to 262 and Verbal IQ from 46 to 300, against a TOGA norming range of 60 to 160. Rosenthal answered that the test's age-equivalent table runs from 0.5 to 16.5 years, that IQ was mental age over chronological age throughout, and that the six second-grade bloomers with a mean posttest IQ of 150 had mental ages of 16.5, 16.5, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 and 8.9. Thorndike's rejoinder was that a scale extrapolated four or five years below the youngest child ever tested is arbitrary rather than merely disputed. The two sides then disagree on something countable. Rosenthal reports that 15 of 17 classrooms showed greater reasoning IQ gains among the bloomers, p = .001, and that dropping the three first-grade classrooms leaves 13 of 14 and dropping the second-grade ones too leaves 10 of 11. Elashoff and Snow report that deleting every pupil scoring below 60 or above 160 on the relevant measure cuts that count to 12 of 17, which is not significant. Their own verdict is no expectancy advantage in grades 3 to 6, and enough suggestion of one in grades 1 and 2 to warrant further research and nothing stronger. Snow returned to this in 1995. As Spitz and as Jussim and Harber both report him, he plotted pretest against posttest reasoning IQ, found the effect gone once scores outside 60 to 160 were dropped, and traced the total-group result to five children whose pretest and posttest pairs were 17 and 110, 18 and 122, 133 and 202, 111 and 208, and 113 and 211. Snow also argued that the median of Raudenbush's 18 effect sizes, 0.035, described them better than the mean of 0.11, and Rosenthal replied with a median of 0.18 for the nine studies with two weeks or less of prior contact. Neither the 1995 exchange nor Wineburg's 1987 critique was obtained here; both are quoted through Spitz, who reprints them with page numbers, and the five score pairs appear independently in Jussim and Harber. Raudenbush's 1984 article is closed at the American Psychological Association and Unpaywall lists no repository copy, so its abstract was read at the journal's own site and its figures are taken from Spitz and from Jussim and Harber. The d = 0.43 arrives by the same route, from their accounts of a 1994 book chapter that has no DOI. The prior-contact moderator is a good theoretical prediction that happened to be confirmed, which is weaker than a prediction registered before the data were seen. This is also a literature about IQ. Teacher expectations predicting grades or behaviour is a separate and larger body of work, and the workplace meta-analyses of Pygmalion training sit at self-fulfilling prophecy, entry 44. The negative direction is the golem effect, entry 141. Thorndike's case against the instrument is set out at observer-expectancy effect, entry 136, which does not carry Jussim and Harber's reply that low reliability makes group differences harder to find rather than easier. The DOI attached to Rosenthal and Jacobson's book across the literature, 10.2307/2092211, resolves to Wilbur Brookover's review of the book in the American Sociological Review. It is kept below because a reader can open it, and it is labelled for what it is.
misreadings: The effect has been absorbed into management training as proof that believing in people makes them better, at a size the research does not support. Four IQ points, in three grades out of eleven, in one school, with the first-year gap resting on 19 children, is the original result. It is also often stated in reverse as the golem effect, where low expectations damage pupils. Rosenthal and Jacobson manipulated positive expectations only, and Jussim and Harber note that instilling inaccurate negative ones would have been unethical, so the study says nothing about that direction. A quieter error is reading the grade labels as the grades in which the children were pretested. The May 1964 testing was done by the previous year's teachers, so the pupils reported as first-graders sat it in kindergarten, which is where the strange low scores are. Retellings compound this. A widely circulated textbook chapter on the study has the pretest given near the beginning of the academic year rather than at the end of the one before. The deepest misreading is treating the question as settled either way. Raudenbush concluded that expectations do influence IQ, Snow and Wineburg concluded that they do not, and Spitz's history of the controversy finds no compelling evidence for any defined method that reliably raises intelligence by manipulating teachers' expectations. The disagreement is about the same 18 experiments and is live.

sources.text: Rosenthal, R., & Jacobson, L. (1968). Pygmalion in the Classroom: Teacher Expectation and Pupils' Intellectual Development. Holt, Rinehart and Winston. The DOI here belongs to Wilbur B. Brookover's review of the book in the American Sociological Review, 34(2), 283, not to the book. No copy of the book was obtained for this entry; searches of the Internet Archive, Unpaywall and the open web found none, and its figures are read off the critics and replies below, which reprint its tables.

Thorndike, R. L. (1968). Reviews: Rosenthal, Robert, and Jacobson, Lenore. Pygmalion in the Classroom. American Educational Research Journal, 5(4), 708-711. Source for the first-year table of IQ gains by grade, for the class of 19 pupils with a mean reasoning score of 31, and for the first-grade reasoning mean of 58. Read from the reprint in chapter VII of Elashoff and Snow's Pygmalion Reconsidered, which also reprints Thorndike's rejoinder from the same journal in 1969.

Rosenthal, R. (1969). Comments: Empirical vs Decreed Validation of Clocks and Tests. American Educational Research Journal, 6(4), 689-691. Rosenthal's answer to Thorndike, and the source for the mental ages of the six second-grade bloomers and for the count of 15 of 17 classrooms. Read from the reprint in chapter VII of Pygmalion Reconsidered.

Elashoff, J. D., & Snow, R. E. (1971). Pygmalion Reconsidered: A Case Study in Statistical Inference. Worthington, Ohio: Charles A. Jones. Reanalysis of the Rosenthal and Jacobson data; read in full. Source for the pretest and posttest counts, the score ranges, the truncated-data classroom count and the chapter V conclusions.

Raudenbush, S. W. (1984). Magnitude of teacher expectancy effects on pupil IQ as a function of the credibility of expectancy induction: A synthesis of findings from 18 experiments. Journal of Educational Psychology, 76(1), 85-97. Closed at the publisher; the abstract was read at the journal's own site at Ovid and the numbers above come through Spitz and through Jussim and Harber.

Spitz, H. H. (1999). Beleaguered Pygmalion: A History of the Controversy Over Claims that Teacher Expectancy Raises Intelligence. Intelligence, 27(3), 199-234. Read in full. Source for Raudenbush's contact gradient, for the quotations from Snow (1995) and Rosenthal (1995), and for the description of the school.

Jussim, L., & Harber, K. D. (2005). Teacher expectations and self-fulfilling prophecies: Knowns and unknowns, resolved and unresolved controversies. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 9(2), 131-155. Read in full from the author copy at Rutgers; the source for the figures quoted from the original study, from Raudenbush's 1984 meta-analysis and from his 1994 re-analysis.

Snow, R. E. (1995). Pygmalion and Intelligence? Current Directions in Psychological Science, 4(6), 169-171. Closed and not obtained; Unpaywall lists no open copy. Quoted here through Spitz, who reproduces the passage with page numbers, and corroborated by Jussim and Harber.
Rosenthal, R. (1995). Critiquing Pygmalion: A 25-Year Perspective. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 4(6), 171-172. Closed and not obtained; quoted here through Spitz.

Wineburg, S. S. (1987). The Self-Fulfillment of the Self-Fulfilling Prophecy. Educational Researcher, 16(9), 28-37. Closed and not obtained; described here as Spitz and as Jussim and Harber report it.

The effects of teacher expectation interventions on teachers' expectations and student achievement: narrative review and meta-analysis. Educational Research and Evaluation, 24(3-5), 180-200. Read in full from the publisher's version deposited at Groningen.
